newsitem.title: CANADA: Suncor has "shot at" 1997 earnings rise - CEO.
newsitem.headline: Suncor has "shot at" 1997 earnings rise - CEO.

text.p: Suncor Energy Inc president and chief executive Richard George said the company still has "a good shot" at posting a year-over-year improvement in its 1997 earnings despite an expected fall in the second quarter.

A month-long shutdown at Suncor's Fort McMurray, Alberta oil sands plant for maintenance and preparation for increased production will result in second quarter-financial results sinking below the prior-year period, George said.
"However, we expect to make up for the production shortfall during the rest of the year," George told the company's annual meeting.

George told shareholders that given the shutdown, it may be difficult to match the past four years of annual earnings gains. But he later told reporters he was still hopeful that a year-over-year rise was achievable.

"But we are actually hopeful -- and it's a hope, it's not a commitment here -- that we will be able to exceed 1996 results in 1997 despite the turnaround," George he said. "I think we've got a good shot at it, but it's not a given, I can tell you that."

George outlined Suncor's growth strategy for the next several years to the annual meeting. He said of the previously announced C$2 billion in capital spending planned for the next four years, C$700 million will occur in 1997.
Two-thirds of this will be spent completing its oil sands plant expansion and preparing its Steepbank mine, scheduled to open in 18 months.

Suncor's methodical growth strategy is split into priorities, the first of which is the expansion of oil sands production beyond 1999 when it is slated to reach 105,000 barrels per day, George said. "We hope to be in a position to discuss detailed plans for oil sands growth some time in the last half of the year," he added.
George gave no further detail on the expansion plans except to say a small team with engineering consultants was looking at options.
Suncor will be in a position to make a final decision on the 50 percent owned Stuart Oil Shale project in Australia in the next two to three months, George told shareholders.
This is the first time a company has commercially developed oil shale worldwide. Suncor is looking at developing the financing for the project right now.

"We think we're going to be able to do that with an exposure of less than C$50 million after tax. So we will have a 50 percent interest in this project but minimize our exposure," George told reporters.
An Australian court decision called the Wik Decision which put a lot of land leases in the country into question will not impact Suncor, George believes.

"We've done all of our title searches and there appears to be no prior aboriginal or native rights associated with our property. However, we are going to check that out fully before we go ahead," George said.
The company is also examining ways to get into refining in the U.S. midwest because of increased output from its oil sands plant.

The Suncor refinery in Sarnia, Ontario, can only manage about 40,000 of the existing oil sands plant's output of 81,000 barrels per day. This output will rise to 85,000 barrels per day after this spring's shutdown and to 105,000 by 1999.
"We actually like a position where we have a dedicated home for a certain portion of that output," George told reporters. The company has direct access to the midwest through two pipelines.
A midwest United States deal could also give Suncor an opportunity to better leverage other types of products put out by the oil sands plant.
